l.t: Your goal is to build your own data centre: a building full of computers, the kind that trains AI models.
You could buy the machines when the day comes. You would rather know what is inside them, so you are building every layer yourself, starting at sand.
Every computer in that building runs on chips, and one AI chip, such as NVIDIA's H100, holds about 80 billion tiny switches. This act builds one of those switch
This is a zoomed-in silicon crystal lattice, refined from sand. By the end of this step, you will learn how to drive a current through it.
Every silicon atom holds four bonds, one to each neighbour. The whole crystal is that one pattern, repeated.
Each bond is a pair of electrons, one contributed by each atom. Both electrons stay locked in the bond.
Tap this atom. Watch what its bond electrons do.
When you tapped it, the bond electrons wobbled and settled back where they were. None of them came loose.
Because every electron is locked in a bond, nothing can move, so nothing can carry a current. Your goal is to make it conduct electricity.
To do that, we dope the crystal (swap a few silicon atoms for a different element, such as phosphorus or boron, which bring extra electrons or holes). Pick one:

In step 1 you doped silicon two ways. Here is one block of each. Your goal is to press them together and find the voltage that pushes a current across the join.
The N block, doped with phosphorus, has free electrons. The P block, doped with boron, has holes, drawn as rings. Both drift around their block.

There is no battery yet. Watch what the carriers (the free electrons and holes) next to the junction do on their own.
The electrons nearest the junction crossed over and filled the nearest holes. No battery pushed them. The N side is crowded with free electrons and the P side h
Each electron that crossed left behind a charged atom that is locked in the crystal and cannot move.
The region around the junction now has no free electrons and no free holes. This region is called the depletion layer (a layer depleted of carriers).
The crossing stopped on its own, because the P side is now slightly negative and the N side slightly positive, and that pushes the next electron back.
Here is that same push, drawn as a hill. An electron has to climb this hill to get across the depletion layer. Watch it slide back down.
Now a battery is wired across the junction so that it pushes the carriers toward the depletion layer. The lamp shows whether any current gets through.
Your goal is to raise the voltage until current flows. Each step up in voltage lowers the hill.
The hill is 0.7 V tall. Below that voltage the electron slid back every time; above it, current flows.
Inside, the battery's − end pushes electrons into the N side, and its + end pulls electrons out of the P side, leaving holes. These new carriers cancel the char
At 0.7 V the layer is too thin to hold them back. Electrons cross the junction and fill holes on the P side, giving off a little heat, while the battery keeps s
If you turn the battery around, the carriers (electrons and holes) get pulled away from the depletion layer instead of being pushed toward it.
Your goal is to turn the voltage all the way up and confirm that nothing flows. Watch the depletion layer and the hill as you go.
The depletion layer got wider and the hill got taller. In this direction, no voltage gets an electron across.

Your diode opens only when the current through it pushes hard enough. A switch needs a separate wire that turns a large current on and off.
This is the junction you built last step: N against P, with a depletion layer between them. Current only crosses it above about 0.7 V.
If you put two of these junctions back to back, you get a switch you can control. That takes three blocks: N, then a thin P, then N.
The emitter is the block that emits (sends out) the electrons. It is small because its only job is to push electrons into the block next to it.
The base is the thin P block in the middle. Every electron the emitter sends out has to cross it.
The collector collects the electrons that make it across. It is wide because it carries the whole current, and a large current produces heat.
From left to right, the blocks are the emitter, the base and the collector. Drag each block into a slot, or tap a block and then a slot.
Each junction builds its own depletion layer, just like the single junction did. Because there are two junctions, there are two barriers, facing opposite ways.
Now we connect a battery across the device, from collector to emitter. Because one of the two barriers always faces the wrong way, the LED stays dark.
You already know how to lower a barrier: push about 0.7 V across it. This second battery does that, from the base down to the emitter.
This voltage acts on the left barrier only. When that barrier narrows, electrons start crossing from the emitter into the base.
Those electrons are now in the base, and the base wire is a way out. Where do they go?
A hundred electrons leave the emitter, one after another. This tally counts where each one ends up.

Start with a block of P-type silicon. It is full of holes and has no spare electrons anywhere.
Now dope a patch at each end into N-type silicon, so that each patch is packed with spare electrons. Drag them in.
Between the two patches is a strip of P silicon with no spare electrons, so nothing can cross this gap. Our whole job is to close this gap on demand.
Two tiles are left: a thin sheet of glass and a metal pad. One of them goes straight onto the silicon, over the gap. Drag it in.
Now place the metal pad on top of the glass. It sits directly over the gap and never touches the silicon. This pad is called the gate.
The two N regions have names. Electrons enter at the source and leave at the drain.
Now wire a battery across them, with plus at the drain and minus at the source, and try to push a current through.

Metal, then glass, then silicon: these three layers form a capacitor (two conducting plates with an insulator between them).
Charging the top plate costs no steady current, because the glass blocks any flow. What does reach the silicon below is the plate's electric field.
If you put a small positive voltage on the gate, the positive plate pushes the holes underneath it downward, away from the glass.
If you keep going, the same field pulls electrons up out of the silicon and holds them against the underside of the glass.
With a little more voltage, that sheet of electrons reaches both N regions, and the source and drain become one unbroken path.
The lamp is lit. Current runs from drain to source through a sheet of electrons that only exists while the gate voltage is held high.Nothing went into the gate
The slider is yours now. If you push the gate voltage higher, the sheet gets denser and more current flows. Your goal is to switch it fully on, above 2.6 V.
Now bring it back down. The sheet breaks the moment the gate voltage drops below 1.2 V. Your goal is to switch it fully off, below 0.3 V.
Your transistor from last step and this new transistor can both stay on all day. Which one is cheaper to hold on?

Four transistors give one answer: the output is 0 only when both inputs are 1. The name for a gate that does this is NAND, short for not both.
If you tie both inputs to one wire, they are always equal. Feed that wire a 1 and the output is 0. The NAND now works as an inverter, also called a NOT gate.
If you put a NAND in front of that NOT gate, the 0 flips back to 1. The pair now outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1, and that is an AND gate.

You already know this one: 5 + 3 = 8. Here you build the circuit that gets there, and check it against the answer you started with.
Here are four lamps in a row. Each lamp holds one bit: a single 0 or 1, lit for 1 and dark for 0.
Each lamp also has a weight: 8, 4, 2, 1. This is place value. The row shows a number: add up the weights of the lit lamps.
This row reads 8 + 4 + 1 = 13. Your goal is to make it read 9.
One lamp can only show 0 or 1. 1 + 1 is 2, which does not fit in a single lamp, so the answer spills into the lamp on its left. That spill is called the carry.
Here is the same sum on paper, in binary (numbers written with only the digits 0 and 1). 5 is 101 and 3 is 011. Work it one column at a time, starting at the ri
Ones column: 1 + 1 = 2. Two does not fit here, so write 0 in this column and pass 1 to the column on the left.
In the twos column, 0 + 1 plus the carried 1 makes 2. In the fours column, 1 + 0 plus the carried 1 makes 2 again. Each time, write 0 and pass 1 left.
Nothing left to add in the eights column, but a carry is still coming in from the right. It lands here as a 1.
The sum row reads 1000. Add the weights of the lit columns: 8. The paper method lands on the answer you already had.
Every column did the same job: add two digits and the carry in, write one digit, and pass any carry left. You will build that job once as a circuit, then copy i

The sum digit is 1 when the two digits differ. The gate that asks "do these differ?" is XOR (exclusive or). There are two here, because the carry in has to be c
The carry asks a different question: were both digits 1? AND answers that. There are two again: one for A and B, and one for the carry in.
There are two ways to produce a carry, and either one is enough. OR (output 1 if either input is 1) merges them into the single carry out.
Your goal is to place the five gates. The caption under each empty box says which question that box answers.
Your five gates are live now. Your goal is to make SUM read 0 while CARRY OUT reads 1.
SUM reads 0 and CARRY OUT reads 1. The column kept 0 and handed the carry to the column on its left, the same move you made on paper.
The five gates now sit inside one box, the full adder. Here it is stamped four times, once per column, in place value order: eights, fours, twos, ones.
Each full adder's carry out feeds the carry in of the full adder on its left, the same way you wrote the carries above the paper sum.
Every carry has to wait for the column on its right, so the answer settles from right to left. Four full adders chained like this are a ripple adder.
The answer row has five lamps: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Four columns hold up to 15, so a bigger sum needs that fifth lamp.

The SR latch remembers because each gate's output keeps the other gate's input where it was, even after you let go.
This is what people mean when they say a computer stores 0s and 1s. Each bit is a loop like this one, holding its wire at 1 or 0 until the power goes off.
This loop is what SRAM is. The cache in a processor, its small fast memory, is millions of these loops, each built with 6 transistors instead of your 8.
One SR latch holds one bit. Four of them side by side hold four bits.
Four latches side by side are a register: a circuit that holds a whole number. These four are holding 11.
Your register holds 4 bits. Eight bits together are a byte, which holds a number from 0 to 255. Memory is counted in bytes, so 16 GB is about 16 billion bytes.
